draft_context.description: Apple iPhone Ultra A bold new entrant The iPhone Ultra is set to usher in the age of the foldable iPhone, and leaks point to a device that has the potential to be truly noteworthy. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Short and sweet The Z Fold 8 is uniquely interesting, and while it may not have the best cameras, it makes foldable fun to use. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Pricing and availability (Image credit: Derrek Lee / Android Central) The iPhone Ultra is slated to make its debut at Apple's launch event on September 9, 2026. The foldable could cost anywhere between $2,000 to $2,500, and we'll have to wait until the event to know the official pricing. But with Apple hiking prices on most of its products in the last two months, it's a given that this year's iPhones will see price increases across the board. Even if the iPhone Ultra is unveiled alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, it may not actually show up at the same time — the latest leaks point to general availability later in the year. Again, that's something we will know definitely on September 9. Given the cost, it is projected that the foldable will be available in limited quantities — much like the Galaxy Z TriFold — and it remains to be seen if it will be sold in all regions simultaneously. Samsung unveiled the Galaxy Z Fold 8 on July 22, 2026, and the foldable retails at $1,899. This is the base model with 256GB of storage, and there's also a 512GB edition that costs $2,099 in the U.S., and a 1TB model that is $2,499. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Design (Image credit: Nicholas Sutrich / Android Central) The iPhone Ultra will be different to every other iPhone thus far, with the foldable design ushering in an entirely new form factor for iOS. Leaks point to the iPhone Ultra having a similar wide-and-short configuration as the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and the passport-style design is definitely intriguing — there's no wonder that other Android manufacturers are emulating a similar style. Leaks point to a 5.5-inch cover panel and a 7.8-inch inner panel, and the iPhone Ultra could be as thin as 4.5mm while unfolded, bringing it in line with the Z Fold 8 and other Android foldables. The design looks a lot like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold , with rounded edges and a flatter profile along the hinge. While Apple introduced a bright orange color with the iPhone 17 Pro , the iPhone Ultra is said to be available in muted colors, including white and black. Just like Android foldables, the iPhone Ultra may see Touch ID housed within the power button as the standard mode of authentication instead of Face ID. The Z Fold 8 gets a 5.5-inch cover panel and a 7.6-inch inner screen, and Samsung managed to deliver IP48 dust and water resistance. Interestingly, one of the biggest selling points of the iPhone Ultra could be a display without anu visible crease. The Find N6 and Vivo X Fold 5 do a fabulous job in this regard — they're better than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra — and with the iPhone Ultra touted to use two layers of ultra-thin glass and a liquid-metal hinge, it is entirely possible that Apple's foldable will debut with a creaseless design, outshining Samsung's Z Fold 8 in this key area. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Hardware (Image credit: Apple / Android Central) The iPhone Ultra will see the biggest battery of any iPhone, and that in itself is exciting. Leaks point to a 4,883mAh battery, and that's similar to what's available on the Z Fold 8. That said, iOS has much better efficiency in general, so the iPhone Ultra should have better battery life, and with Apple touted to switch to a 2nm node, battery life could get an additional boost. The iPhone Ultra is likely to use a similar arrangement, and leaks point to two 48MP cameras, without a dedicated tele lens. We'll need to wait and see if that pans out, but as someone who uses the telephoto lens constantly, I would like to see this on the foldable. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Software (Image credit: Derrek Lee / Android Central) Software makes a big difference on a foldable, with the added real estate ideal to multitask. This is a priority in iOS 27, and there's no doubt that the iPhone Ultra will get a lot of the same features that we've seen on Android foldables over the last two years, including a task bar, floating windows, and multitasking features. Samsung does a good job in this area with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and I'm interested in seeing how the iPhone Ultra will hold up against Samsung's foldable. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Which should you buy? (Image credit: AppleTrack) While foldables have been around for the better part of a decade now, they're still pretty niche. That will change with the introduction of the iPhone Ultra; say what you will about Apple, but the brand has an unmatched ability to grab attention, and interest in foldables will skyrocket following the iPhone Ultra launch. Now, whether this will translate to sales is another thing entirely, but if you're an iPhone user and wanted to switch to a foldable, you don't need to wait long to get one running iOS. While Samsung got a lot right with the Z Fold 8, it doesn't do nearly enough to convince iOS users to move to Android in any meaningful numbers. Apple iPhone Ultra A bold new entrant The iPhone Ultra is set to launch soon, and with a similar design as the Z Fold 8 but with iOS, it could just be the device that convinces iPhone users to switch to a foldable. For those who want a full security setup, Eufy is also launching an eight-channel NVR system with 2K security cameras. I’m not sure how many NVR features will need MindBase to function, but Anker says the wired, fully contained kit can handle auto framing, smart video searches, cross-camera tracking and 24/7 recording.

draft_context.source_title: How Sonos rebooted itself
draft_context.description: Today, I’m talking with Tom Conrad, the CEO of Sonos. Tom and I have known each other for a long time — he was the chief technology officer of Pandora, VP of product at Snap, and the chief product officer of Quibi. He was also on the board at Sonos during its disastrous 2024 app redesign that threatened to crash the entire brand. Tom took over as interim CEO to right the ship during that period, and then took the permanent role just about a year ago. As you’ll hear him say, he thinks Sonos is fully out of that period now, and on to its next chapter with a huge product and platform launch called Sonos 27 . Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . I mean, come on, you all listen to the show. That is all the most Decoder bait imaginable. I have been dying to have Tom on the show to talk about how the board decided to move on from previous CEO Patrick Spence, how he diagnosed the issues inside the company, and what decisions he made to fix them. Those fixes involved a lot of big changes: to the company’s structure, its product lineup, and how it thinks about itself and what its product fundamentally is. That’s that new platform, Sonos 27, which you’ll hear Tom call a new foundation for the company that makes every Sonos product work better as part of a system. There’s a lot here, including how AI assistants can work across the system, the idea of having a mesh network of little computers in your home disguised as speakers, and of course, the testy relationship between Sonos and Google, which means Google’s Gemini assistant isn’t available on Sonos devices. Oh, and of course we got into the weeds about smart home standards, because I am a smart home nerd and simply cannot help myself. But to his credit, Tom was willing to nerd out with me, and I think this conversation is pretty fun because of it. Okay: Sonos CEO Tom Conrad. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Tom Conrad, you’re the CEO of Sonos. Welcome to Decoder . Thank you. As they say, it’s so great to be here. I am just going to say, finally, I have been asking you to be on the show for at least a year, if not before. I think the first time I met you was in the back of a car at CES when you were at Pandora. Sounds right. One hundred years ago. One hundred years ago. We were children. [Laughs] We were little babies. That car was driven by a human driver. That’s how far back it was. That’s right. And then you took a turn through Quibi. You and I talked through that, and now you’re at Sonos. As you know, I’m a huge fan of Sonos. We had your predecessor, Patrick Spence, on the show a bunch of times . Many things have happened, so I just want to start at the very beginning of this. You’re about a year into being the permanent CEO of Sonos. You have a bunch of news to announce. Just tell us what you think Sonos is today. What is your conception of this company? When I came in the door, one of my earliest observations was that the company behaved like it was 100 percent hardware, but we’re really 100 percent hardware and 100 percent software. And if you get either one of those even a little bit wrong, the impact is tremendous. So how does that show up really day-to-day? It was about returning the company to the idea that Sonos doesn’t make these individual products, but we really make one thing — we make the Sonos system. It all has to hang together in a cohesive, interesting, and valuable way, or we’re just not doing the work. There’s been a bunch of basic blocking and tackling, of course, both operationally and in the work that we’re doing in the product family. But at the highest level, returning the company to the idea that we are a system for audio in the home has been the highest-level mantra. When you say come into the company, do you mean as a board member or as the CEO? I mean, let’s start the starter pistol in January of 2025, 18 months ago, when I stepped in first as interim CEO and then was lucky enough six months later to be asked to take the job more permanently. The reason I asked that question is that you obviously have two different views of the company in different roles. We did have former CEO Patrick Spence on several occasions, and he said something very similar to me when he first took over — that Sonos was stuck in its ways. It was really focused on very, very slow iterations of hardware. He tried very hard to push the metabolism of the company to be much faster, and he talked about that very openly with me. That led eventually to what I think is a moment of true crisis: the app launch. It was a disaster. The system stopped working. That’s when you came in to right the ship. Tell me about that gap. You came in, and you said this company thinks it’s a hardware company. That’s what your predecessor had been saying, but it went sideways in big, meaningful ways. Tell me about that moment and why you think it was the same conception even when you came in. So as you describe, I’ve been involved with the company going back almost 20 years. We brought Pandora to Sonos in 2007, I think, and I was able to get to know the company as a partner before I got to know it as a board member. I came onto the board in 2016 right as Patrick became CEO. So from the vantage point of a board member, I got to participate in Patrick’s chapter. I guess the way I would characterize his high-order thinking about the company in those early days was that, as you described, he wanted to turn the company into a product execution machine with an emphasis on hardware products. We call them NPIs, or new product introductions. In the chapter before him, it was sometimes years between new Sonos products. Spence said, “Look, we’re going to make a company that knows how to ship a couple of great new products a year.” And he did that. I mean, the company has reliably shipped a couple of great products, hardware products, every year, for close to a decade now. Sometimes, when you energize an organization around an idea, there are unintended consequences. I think one unintended consequence of that framing was that the company became very focused on the individual products, one at a time. Even as a board member, I received Roam as a portable speaker with a certain amount of battery life, waterproofing, and Bluetooth connectivity. I didn’t really think about it as a member of the Sonos system. Even with the software work that we did, and with every product that we make, there is a tremendous amount of software effort and innovation that goes into them. But even the software that we made was very focused on the individual NPIs. “What can we do in software to differentiate Move 2 from other speakers in that category?” What was hard to do, and what was hard to prioritize in the company, was horizontal slices of software experiences that benefited all of the platform. So, in a way, I think some of that debt accumulated, and the company thought that the antidote was to recreate the app experience. And as you know, we made a bunch of mistakes at that moment. I’m really proud of the fact that I think we’re well beyond that chapter now, but we could have been much more thoughtful about how we qualified that product in the real world. We could have been much more thoughtful about how we rolled it out to customers. We could have, candidly, I think, examined the original impetus in the first place. It was very Sonos-motivated. We wanted to put the app on a modern architecture to make us more nimble. In my chapter at Sonos, I’m really trying to bring it all back to how we can focus on the customer first. I’m so inspired by talking to people on social media and in my inbox, and people in the industry, like you, about how we show up and solve the real problems that are happening in real households. I’m so excited about the things we’re going to talk to you about today because I think they’re really an answer to many of those questions. If you’re a listener, you know I’m familiar with Tom. The man’s on Threads doing customer support every day. And actually, I should not take advantage of this. I hold myself back from asking you for direct customer support all the time. Anytime. The way that you can tell it’s actually me and not our crackerjack social team is that I often will let a Thread die before I should or fail to follow up with someone. So if we were executing perfectly on that, you would know it was fake Tom, but it’s real Tom, and I do it when I can, but sometimes imperfectly. At least it’s not an AI avatar Tom. That’s when we know it’s going to go sideways. [Laughs] That’s right. I know you’re a Decoder fan, so I’m going to make you sit in this for just one more moment because I find all of this to be really fascinating. The app shipped, and the feedback was immediately and intensely negative. Many, many things were broken. Speakers weren’t working at weddings. This is a time of massive crisis. The company goes to resolve it, but then you’re on the board, and it’s clear that there’s going to be a leadership transition, that Patrick needs to go, and we need a new CEO. You’re going to be the interim CEO. Tell us about that process. Very, very few people will ever be in that kind of process or get insight into that process. What happened? What were the steps? Well, I guess you start by saying that the last thing as a board that you want to do is to remove a CEO, particularly one who had as many successes as Patrick had. But I think as we looked at the company’s progress recovering from the app crisis, and frankly the tenor of the conversation inside the company, we just decided that for this kind of step-function improvement we needed on some of these dimensions, we had to make some changes in leadership, and that included a CEO change. It was a wild experience for me because, I’ll tell you, at no point in the decade leading up to that day in January did I imagine that I might end up the CEO of Sonos. But in the process, the board asked if I’d be willing to step in on an interim basis, and it was an easy yes for me. It’s a cliché, but I’m a customer, and I love this product. There was a Sonos Move in the room when my daughter was born. You talked about weddings. I was watching friends and colleagues on the internet, frustrated by their experience. I wanted to come in and fix it. Of course, as a board member, I felt some real culpability in it. So [I was] thrilled at the chance to come in. When you’re an interim CEO, the assignment is really to keep the wheels on. The assignment at Sonos specifically was to right the ship. So during the period when the board was doing their comprehensive search for the person that they would ultimately decide was the right choice for the company, it was really easy for me to show up and just do that hard work of trying to get the company back on track. While I never imagined that I would land in this seat, I feel so blessed that it happened. I do love this job and continue to love the company and the team, and I’m so excited about the things we’re doing for our customers. Very few people are going to get an interview to become the CEO of Sonos. I imagine at some point you went from being the interim CEO to wanting to become the permanent CEO. What was that process like? Did you write a memo? Was there a pitch deck? What were the steps? Yeah, so there were a couple of pitch moments that the board asked me, completely reasonably, to engage in the process of applying for the job in the same way that all of the other talented candidates that they spoke to engaged. And so I took a personality test. Wait, you did? Yeah. With the letters? Oh, yeah. Like an ENTJ or whatever? Oh, yeah. One of the letter things, sure. They wanted to know what they were getting. Do they know that that is basically just like astrology? Someone should tell them. You know what? Yep, yep. I presented my vision for the company more than once, and I had the incredible advantage of being inside the four walls of the company and deeply understanding what was working and what wasn’t, and the things that we needed to do to get to this next chapter. It was a period of intense, intense work for me and everybody around me at the company, and more than a little anxiety about how it was going to turn out. It was so fun, though, to get the call and then to just immediately be able to pivot at least a fraction of the work from the entirely tactical to the much more strategic, to begin to talk about what kind of company we are going to build together in this next chapter. When it was announced that you would become the permanent CEO, even when you were the interim CEO, my reaction was, “Oh, this makes sense.” To use a football analogy, football teams hire defensive head coaches and offensive head coaches, and they come from one side of the ball or the other. It was just obvious: “Oh, this company needs a software CEO, and Tom is a software guy.” You’re describing a situation where obviously it’s both. You’ve got hardware and software together, but that was the light that went off in my head — “Oh, this is a software person coming in to fix a big software problem.” Is that how you saw it initially? Yeah, my career started with selling personal computers in 1986 or something, at the original Micro Center. If you’ve ever been to a Micro Center, it’s one of the few remaining big-box retailers for computers. So at the original Micro Center in Columbus, Ohio, at 16 years old, I walked into the CEO’s office and said, “I want to work here.” So from my earliest days, I was sitting with early adopters of personal computers and watching their struggles to understand the technology and put it to use in their lives. I became an engineer and a product designer out of a desire to help people learn to use these products. And that’s really what’s motivated me through my entire career: how do I help teams make great experiences? So while it’s true that I’m a software person, 35 years in the business, my identity really is as a product designer. And I’d like to think that the board imagined that, yes, they needed a software person, but they needed somebody who could holistically look at the opportunity across hardware and software and help the team get there. You appear to be through it now. There’s a big stack of announcements here, including MCP integration. I’ve got a lot of questions about all that. When you became the permanent CEO 18 months ago, you said you immediately shifted strategy. What brought that into focus for you? “Oh, this is actually a software platform with hardware components”? Was that instinct? Was it research? Was it, “I’m getting through this app process, and that is becoming revealed to me”? How did that work? I think by disposition I’m a fairly right-brained person, and I have this intuitive feeling — creative, or whatever the words are, not as quantitative. But my first job out of college was at Apple, and I think even from the early days when I was there, we talked about the intersection of the arts and humanities and the sciences. I think one lesson of my career has been that you really do have an obligation to bring both a quant and a qual assessment to most things that pass your desk. So the development of our strategy was very much like that. Yes, there was an intuitive sense about what the right answer for Sonos was that was built up from my experience as a customer by observing our customers and talking to them through the years. A piece of that is a perspective about where the puck is going, of course. But I do have access to piles and piles and piles of data about how our products behave in the real world, how our customers interact with them, what they use, what they don’t use, and lots of people around me in the organization who can bring that quantitative framing. I think one advantage I had over other CEO candidates was that I could bring some of that horsepower to bear on the story that I shared with the board about my vision for the future of the company. You’ve made some changes. It’s time for the Decoder questions. You have restructured the company. There have been a few rounds of layoffs. How big is Sonos today? We’re about 1,500 people. And how is that structured? So the company that I stepped into was divided into business units. We had a team that was focused on home. We had a team that was focused on the professional opportunity, a team that was focused on home theater, and so on. While there’s something to be said for P&L responsibilities, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, there’s something to be said for that approach at a certain scale. I think that my appraisal was that we were sub-scale for the inefficiencies that creep in. We have the almost guaranteed duplication of effort across the silos. What’s more, if you imagine that the product is really the system, the idea that your portables team sits far away from your home theater team, and sits far away from your plugged-in speakers team, is almost surely going to run counter to the kind of progress that you’re trying to motivate. And so very quickly, within three weeks of my arrival, we reorganized the company into a functional model. So my leadership team today, of course, has a finance organization, a legal organization, a sales organization, and a marketing organization. But the product team now shows up as represented by hardware, software, and global supply chain operations, so leaders across each of those things. And what that allows us to do is to assemble cross-functional teams, or matrix-style teams, to invest in the initiatives that are of the highest priority to our customers and to the business at any given moment. And we can flex that up and down and side to side as our needs change. We might, for an interval, be very focused on this part of the portfolio over here, and then we might be able to move to focusing on a different corner of the portfolio. No one has to get a new boss, and people can fluidly move from these things and get new opportunities to learn. It just strikes me as a much more appropriate organizational structure for our current stage. You’re describing the shift from a divisional structure to a vastly more functional structure. Yes. That’s Apple, right? Yep, sure. Everyone comes up, and there’s one big product meeting. You obviously make a lot of software. I’ve described you as a software CEO. It seems like the software industry is in a moment of existential crisis about how software is made, about what a product manager versus an engineer versus a designer do. Are you still in the classic structures of building software? Or has AI completely upended what you’re doing? No, we’re as deep in this as anyone. What’s been really fun for me over the course of the last year is to watch the software engineering team go from thoughtful skepticism to pretty deep embrace, if I’m honest. Some of that is on the back of just how dramatically the tools have evolved over the course of the last 12 months, certainly. I think almost everyone in the industry went home at the holidays at the tail end of 2025, coming into 2026, and came back just gobsmacked by how much progress the frontier labs were making on agentic coding, and it’s been a real accelerant for us. As complex as this transition is, I’m really excited about being able to help our engineers navigate what’s a pretty fundamental sea change in the way that this kind of infrastructure gets built, and it’s fun to get to be a part of that at this moment. Did you break up the classic PM, designer, and engineer triad? Or is that still the core building block? We still have all three, but it blurs particularly as the designers and the product managers can be prototypers at a really high level with incredible efficiency. It’s exciting to see how quickly they can communicate their ideas now in a medium that just didn’t exist at all for them a year ago. We’re at the turn, right? You came in, you restructured the company, you identified a new thesis for the company. Today you’re here to talk about all the new news. Do you think you’re through it? Do you think the existing customers have forgiven you for the app mess? Do you think the brand has been restored? Yeah, as we’ve been saying, I think that there’s the quant and there’s the qual. The quant is green across the board. Performance, reliability, customer care interactions, social tone, NPS — these things are all restored to levels that we enjoyed before any of that happened. On the qualitative side, I love the fact that I can show up on Reddit or on social media broadly and engage with our customers and have a constructive conversation about things that they’re excited that we’re doing, and things where we’re still disappointing an individual customer on some dimension. I think that at some level, maybe this game is never over; you’re just always trying to polish off the remaining rough edges of everything that you do. So I have a real critic’s eye when I look at the work that we do, and if I ever let that slip, a customer will remind me of where the work remains. And so, yes, I think in every measurable way it’s behind us, but it’s a “never forget” chapter for the company. That brings me to the other Decoder question: how do you make decisions? What’s your framework? Well, I don’t think you bring just one framework to every decision. So we talk about, for example, product decisions. As an idea moves through its lifecycle from its days as an early little sapling that you have to care and tend to, through final mass production for a hardware object, and out into the channels, I think how you think about [each of those] decisions is different. So in the earliest days, I really tried to protect the creativity of the company and to not let the antibodies of doubt and critique erode an idea before it’s had a chance to express itself in a way that anybody could get excited about. That means creating room for risk-taking, creativity, qualitative assessment, and prototyping before you get to the details of the business case and the hard trade-offs that you make on a journey from an idea to something you can actually ship. But of course, as the programs roll along and they take on more and more financial investment and organizational risk, as more and more people aggregate into the product, you become, I think, just naturally much more quantitative in your analysis of the decisions. And you ask the teams to bring a really thoughtful, detailed description of the puts and takes and the risks associated with it, and you use that to help you make your decisions. But maybe on top of all of that, you just have to hire great people. I mean, you just do, and you have to put them on teams that are an appropriate size for the task at hand. I think it’s going to be very, very difficult for any CEO or any leadership team to make great decisions if the people who aren’t bringing the ideas themselves aren’t great. So I suppose it starts with the right people in the seats. The reason I ask that question in that way is that, I think, the decision you made that is most emblematic to me of changing from a divisional structure with individual P&Ls to a more functional structure, and thinking about the platform as a whole, was the decision to kill a product that I believe was called Pinewood. It was a set-top box that was going to integrate all the streaming services. This was well reported by former Verge reporter Chris Welch , who’s now at Bloomberg. The thing that really struck me about that was if you had a division that was focused on soundbars, the only place that division could go was to compete with Roku. And all the reporting that we had before suggested that the soundbar division was growing because the attach rate for soundbars with new TVs is 100 percent. Everyone knows the speakers in their TVs are bad. It’s a great business, and we’re for sure the best product in the category. So if you want to grow, which is the big thing, you’re going to be like, “How do we grow? And you say, “Well, I got to beat Roku.” And then now you’re just off doing that. You came in, and you just ended that, and I thought, “Oh, this is not just a decision to end a product line; this is also a decision about the strategy of the company. Because if you’re going to go compete with Roku, you’ve got to be a different company.” That’s my view of it. Is that how you saw it? Like so many things, these decisions do have more than one dimension that you evaluate. A big part of that decision, candidly, was that we were spread too thin across too many things, and I didn’t believe that we could be exceptional at all of them. I wanted to return us to focus on the thing that allows us to be most differentiated in the competitive set, and that’s the incredible systemness of the product, the audio experience that we can deliver, and attending to what, at the time, was a very long list of things that our customers were explicitly asking us for. I think if we were, putatively, actually working on a set-top box at that moment, another thing that I might have wondered about was whether our desire to make this particular product came from our customer or did it come from some sort of internally sourced sense of business opportunity? And I think companies get in a lot of trouble when the thing that comes first is the model and the thing that comes second is the product. I certainly feel a sense of obligation to constantly be evaluating new business opportunities for the company, new business models for the company, sure. But I want them to always start from a place of what we really see in the market from customers. I’m not sure that they were saying we want a high-end streaming box that is somehow the love child of an Apple TV and a Roku. Although that love child… I would be very worried about that love child. Why does this product have 200GB of storage for no identifiable reason, but also shows me ads at all times? We’ll set that aside. I ask that because I want to talk to you about all the news here. The news here is a bunch of big bets. You’ve got Sonos 27. That is the new name of what you were calling an audio operating system that has something in it called Sonos Fabric. Boy, I know you know me. I’m ready to go on all these names and all these ideas. In there, somewhere, is MCP support. There’s a big idea about assistants that I want to talk about. You’re cashing some chips, right? Yeah. You’re saying, ”Okay, here’s a big new idea. Trust us. We’re going to get it right this time.” You’re ready for it. Yeah, I feel very ready. They’ve got great reviews; they have great noise cancelling. They’re super comfortable, and they look great. We’re really proud of the product, but they weren’t thoughtfully integrated into the Sonos ecosystem. I mean, at launch you could swap to one of our soundbars, not even all of our soundbars. I think it was the most visible expression of the missed opportunity of that moment for the company to always remember that the products that we make are part of the Sonos system, not individual offerings. So we ended up with a great pair of headphones, but honestly, I mean, you review them all the time; there are lots of great headphones. When we set out to take all the lessons that we learned from Ace to design Ace Ultra, at the very top of that list is that we have to do the hard thing. These headphones have to be able to show up in your home as a part of the system, and the model through which you invoke your headphones has to be completely seamless and delightful. We built an entirely new hardware platform for Ace Ultra called Headphone Engine 2, and it unlocks this capability at the hardware level. And then in Sonos OS 27, we built virtualization so that any one of the speakers in your home can deliver the audio platform to that speaker but can also act as a proxy for your headphones, which don’t have the horsepower to run the full stack — it would kill battery life, et cetera. Now with Ace Ultra, you’ll be able to link your headphones to your Sonos system, walk up to a speaker that’s playing, press a button on your headphones, and the music will jump from the speaker into your headphones. No Bluetooth, no phone. You’ll be able to walk around your whole house, enjoy the music, come to another speaker, press the button again, and it will jump to that speaker using some BLA location-sensing stuff that we’ve developed. It’s super magical. It’s the one job that we had and didn’t deliver on with Ace. We’re really excited to get it out into the market. Analogous to that on the home theater side is, as you mentioned, that we’re making all of our portable speakers — Sonos Play, Sonos Move — capable of being rear channels for home theater. That sounds really easy. Maybe people will even be like, “Why wasn’t that always possible?” But to your point about the deep technology of it, the way that we achieve high-fidelity, low-latency surround experiences in the living room is by directly bonding our rear channel speakers and subwoofer to the soundbar on a proprietary network, not through your access point. So for a speaker to seamlessly hop between being part of your Sonos system as a music node and part of your Sonos system as a surround channel means that you have to do a real-time reconfiguration of that networking stack, and you have to know when to do it. We’re using accelerometers in the product to actually know that you’ve picked it up and set it down in a new location. We’re using Sonos’ positioning system, which is ultrasonic signaling, to broadcast to the room, “Hey, is there a soundbar here?” Ultrasonic comes back saying, “I’m here.” They negotiate position, left and right, and distance, so that they can optimize the surround sound experience. You pick it up again, you take it back to the kitchen, and it’s a regular speaker again. All happens magically, no use of the app. It’s pretty cool. Answer my question on headphones, though. This is my big worry. You’ve got really cool headphones. They have a feature that no one else can ship, and Apple’s going to say, “Look, our new AirPods have Siri AI in them.” You can just say, “Show me what I’m looking at,” and a picture will be taken automatically and something will happen. We’ll get over the privacy implications of that, but that’s a collapse of the headphone market. Maybe. I mean, headphones come in all kinds of form factors today: over-ear, in-ear, cuffs, wireless, wired. So I do think it’s a market where people choose different form factors for different tasks. We’re really focused on this personal in-the-home listening — what do you do when the baby’s asleep? What do you do when you want to move the party from the kitchen to the den while you relax for the evening? We think that there’s a bunch of really interesting use cases there that other people aren’t paying attention to. I think, broadly, over the course of the next couple of years, we’re going to get all kinds of adventurous wackadoodle consumer electronics that are connected to this new emerging AI universe. Most of them will be a swing and a miss. Of course, we’ve already seen some of those. So it’s a little hard to speculate, I think, about which of these things, if any, is going to have its iPod moment or its iPhone moment or whatever. What do you think is going to happen? I think we’re going to see a replay of what happened when the headphone jack got taken away. The headphone jack was an open interconnect. There was a really vibrant market for all kinds of headphones, and a bunch of those companies don’t exist anymore. The high-end wired headphones, for phones anyway, have mostly gone away, and you have a bunch of medium Bluetooth competitors, but the phone makers have largely taken that with first-party products. Now, you have your products at the high end competing with really high-end noise-canceling products from Bose and Sony and whoever, and that is the airplane set. The lack of the open interconnect has really killed the vibrancy of the low and middle end of the market. Okay, well, there’s one big thing they can do to make sure the high end belongs to them, and it’s to integrate AI in very specific ways directly into their operating system. We’ll see how that plays out. There’s also a thing that’s different this time: there’s a vastly more energized European regulatory environment. Who knows how this will play out? Sure. I can’t tell you, but all that stuff is a swirl, and you’re a headphone maker, and it seems like different headphone makers are taking different approaches to this. The only counter that I might offer is that there’s a lot of talk about the walled garden of the Bluetooth advantages that the platform companies have. But I would say even without the European regulators, it’s notable that something like the Meta Glasses can have a reasonable, I think, commercially viable set of experiences that are principally powered by compute that lives on your phone and still deliver conversational AI that is mediated by a Bluetooth connection, admittedly behind some of the obstacles that you’re describing. But those obstacles aren’t so profound that clever companies aren’t figuring out how to work within those constraints. I’m very curious to see how that plays out. It doesn’t seem like it’s in focus. Again, probably because, as you say, none of the products are in focus. No one knows what a hit product here looks like, so you might as well let a thousand flowers bloom and then radically constrict the market. Yeah, sure. Tom, I’ve burned just a ton of your time. I think you can tell I could talk to you for ages and ages about all kinds of things. Super fun. Tell us what’s next for Sonos. When does all this stuff ship? So I think by the time this airs, we’ll have announced all of this to the world. We’re having a big event in New York to share Sonos OS 27, Sonos Voice 27, and the Ace Ultra and Beam Ultra. We can’t wait to get this stuff out into the world and begin to hear what our customers do with all of these exciting new products. Many of the software features are going to be available in early access, which will mean our customers will opt into them, be able to give us feedback, and we’ll be able to observe the telemetry that comes back from their homes and make sure that we’re delivering exactly the experience that we want. We’re excited about the moment of co-creation that’s around the corner for us. As we talked about at the top of the hour, Sonos 27 is absolutely a nod to the fact that we intend to keep doing this until the sun burns out. There’ll be Sonos 28 and 29 and 30 and beyond. That’s great. All right, I’ve got to ask you at the end: I have ceiling speakers in my kitchen. They’re connected to a Sonos Amp. There’s a Google Home Hub right there, and it’s broken. I can’t ask it to play music in the kitchen. When are you going to fix that for me? I’m ending on tech support. All right. I don’t know the answer, but I’d love to figure it out for you. I know the right folks to call, so let’s get you connected. We’re going to have a Decoder roundtable. If your listeners have similar kinds of problems, we’ve got great people to help them, and we always like to hear from you. You can find me on social pretty easily. Usually I end by inviting people back, but I’m saying we’ve got to fix it, and then we’re going to talk about what it took to fix it. That’s the plan. All right. Right on. Tom, this is great. Thank you so much, man. This was super fun. Thank you. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! ]]>
paragraphs: Today, I’m talking with Tom Conrad, the CEO of Sonos. Tom and I have known each other for a long time — he was the chief technology officer of Pandora, VP of product at Snap, and the chief product officer of Quibi. He was also on the board at Sonos during its disastrous 2024 app redesign that threatened to crash the entire brand.

Tom took over as interim CEO to right the ship during that period, and then took the permanent role just about a year ago. As you’ll hear him say, he thinks Sonos is fully out of that period now, and on to its next chapter with a huge product and platform launch called Sonos 27 .

I mean, come on, you all listen to the show. That is all the most Decoder bait imaginable. I have been dying to have Tom on the show to talk about how the board decided to move on from previous CEO Patrick Spence, how he diagnosed the issues inside the company, and what decisions he made to fix them.

Those fixes involved a lot of big changes: to the company’s structure, its product lineup, and how it thinks about itself and what its product fundamentally is. That’s that new platform, Sonos 27, which you’ll hear Tom call a new foundation for the company that makes every Sonos product work better as part of a system.

There’s a lot here, including how AI assistants can work across the system, the idea of having a mesh network of little computers in your home disguised as speakers, and of course, the testy relationship between Sonos and Google, which means Google’s Gemini assistant isn’t available on Sonos devices.

article.title: Apple gặp rắc rối với iPhone Ultra trước ngày ra mắt?
article.summary: Cụ thể, sản lượng iPhone Ultra chỉ đạt vài trăm chiếc mỗi ngày vào cuối tháng 8, trong khi Apple cần sản xuất hàng chục nghìn chiếc mỗi ngày để đáp ứng nhu cầu. Mặc dù Apple và các nhà cung cấp đang nỗ lực tăng cường sản xuất, nhưng quá trình này có thể mất thời gian.
article.dek: Cụ thể, sản lượng iPhone Ultra chỉ đạt vài trăm chiếc mỗi ngày vào cuối tháng 8, trong khi Apple cần sản xuất hàng chục nghìn chiếc mỗi ngày để đáp ứng nhu cầu.
article.hook: Cụ thể, sản lượng iPhone Ultra chỉ đạt vài trăm chiếc mỗi ngày vào cuối tháng 8, trong khi Apple cần sản xuất hàng chục nghìn chiếc mỗi ngày để đáp ứng nhu cầu.

sections.heading: Bối cảnh: điều gì đang đổi
sections.body: Cụ thể, sản lượng iPhone Ultra chỉ đạt vài trăm chiếc mỗi ngày vào cuối tháng 8, trong khi Apple cần sản xuất hàng chục nghìn chiếc mỗi ngày để đáp ứng nhu cầu. Mặc dù Apple và các nhà cung cấp đang nỗ lực tăng cường sản xuất, nhưng quá trình này có thể mất thời gian. Nếu tình hình không cải thiện nhanh chóng, việc sở hữu iPhone Ultra sẽ trở nên khó khăn, đặc biệt trong những tuần đầu sau khi ra mắt.

sections.heading: Các nguồn đang khớp nhau ở đâu
sections.body: Tiêu chuẩn cao của Apple dành cho iPhone Ultra đang làm khó các đối tác sản xuất.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Nguyên nhân chính dẫn đến sản lượng thấp là do tiêu chuẩn kiểm soát chất lượng cao mà Apple đang áp dụng. Công ty đã tiến hành thêm một đợt chạy thử và quy trình kiểm tra xác thực vào tháng 8, làm chậm quá trình sản xuất thương mại. Hai yếu tố quan trọng mà Apple chú trọng là hiệu suất bản lề và độ phẳng của màn hình, vốn yêu cầu thử nghiệm trong điều kiện khắc nghiệt hơn so với các đối thủ.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Ban đầu, Apple đặt mục tiêu bán khoảng 7 - 8 triệu chiếc iPhone Ultra trước khi kết thúc năm 2026, sau đó nâng lên khoảng 10 triệu chiếc. Tuy nhiên, với sản lượng thấp như hiện nay, mục tiêu của Apple có thể gặp thách thức. Hơn nữa, iPhone Ultra cần thêm thời gian để đánh giá độ bền, điều mà Galaxy Z Fold8 đang có nhiều lợi thế.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Việc Apple cần thêm các bước kiểm soát chất lượng iPhone Ultra được cho là bắt nguồn từ các trục trặc sản xuất và vấn đề nguồn cung. Công ty đã gặp phải nhiều khó khăn với vật liệu bản lề, thậm chí dẫn đến việc điện thoại phát ra tiếng lạch cạch. Những trở ngại này có thể khiến lịch trình ra mắt của iPhone Ultra khác biệt hoàn toàn so với iPhone 18 Pro và 18 Pro Max. Mặc dù không trì hoãn ngày giới thiệu, nhưng có khả năng việc đặt trước và giao hàng sẽ bị trì hoãn đến cuối tháng 10 hoặc đầu tháng 11 giống như những gì mà iPhone X đã gặp vào năm 2017, thậm chí một số nguồn tin còn cho rằng việc ra mắt iPhone Ultra có thể bị đẩy lùi đến mùa xuân năm sau.

draft_context.source_title: Apple gặp rắc rối với iPhone Ultra trước ngày ra mắt?
draft_context.description: Chiếc iPhone màn hình gập đầu tiên của Apple đang gặp vấn đề sản xuất nghiêm trọng, khiến nguồn cung ban đầu có thể rất hạn chế.
paragraphs: Cụ thể, sản lượng iPhone Ultra chỉ đạt vài trăm chiếc mỗi ngày vào cuối tháng 8, trong khi Apple cần sản xuất hàng chục nghìn chiếc mỗi ngày để đáp ứng nhu cầu. Mặc dù Apple và các nhà cung cấp đang nỗ lực tăng cường sản xuất, nhưng quá trình này có thể mất thời gian. Nếu tình hình không cải thiện nhanh chóng, việc sở hữu iPhone Ultra sẽ trở nên khó khăn, đặc biệt trong những tuần đầu sau khi ra mắt.
Tiêu chuẩn cao của Apple dành cho iPhone Ultra đang làm khó các đối tác sản xuất

Nguyên nhân chính dẫn đến sản lượng thấp là do tiêu chuẩn kiểm soát chất lượng cao mà Apple đang áp dụng. Công ty đã tiến hành thêm một đợt chạy thử và quy trình kiểm tra xác thực vào tháng 8, làm chậm quá trình sản xuất thương mại. Hai yếu tố quan trọng mà Apple chú trọng là hiệu suất bản lề và độ phẳng của màn hình, vốn yêu cầu thử nghiệm trong điều kiện khắc nghiệt hơn so với các đối thủ.

Ban đầu, Apple đặt mục tiêu bán khoảng 7 - 8 triệu chiếc iPhone Ultra trước khi kết thúc năm 2026, sau đó nâng lên khoảng 10 triệu chiếc. Tuy nhiên, với sản lượng thấp như hiện nay, mục tiêu của Apple có thể gặp thách thức. Hơn nữa, iPhone Ultra cần thêm thời gian để đánh giá độ bền, điều mà Galaxy Z Fold8 đang có nhiều lợi thế.

Việc Apple cần thêm các bước kiểm soát chất lượng iPhone Ultra được cho là bắt nguồn từ các trục trặc sản xuất và vấn đề nguồn cung. Công ty đã gặp phải nhiều khó khăn với vật liệu bản lề, thậm chí dẫn đến việc điện thoại phát ra tiếng lạch cạch. Những trở ngại này có thể khiến lịch trình ra mắt của iPhone Ultra khác biệt hoàn toàn so với iPhone 18 Pro và 18 Pro Max. Mặc dù không trì hoãn ngày giới thiệu, nhưng có khả năng việc đặt trước và giao hàng sẽ bị trì hoãn đến cuối tháng 10 hoặc đầu tháng 11 giống như những gì mà iPhone X đã gặp vào năm 2017, thậm chí một số nguồn tin còn cho rằng việc ra mắt iPhone Ultra có thể bị đẩy lùi đến mùa xuân năm sau.

Sự chậm trễ này có thể mang lại lợi thế cho các đối thủ cạnh tranh của Apple, như Samsung, Huawei và Xiaomi, khi họ có thêm thời gian để chiếm lĩnh thị trường. Việc trì hoãn kéo dài là điều không thể chấp nhận và người tiêu dùng sẽ đánh giá cao một chiếc điện thoại gập bền bỉ, đặc biệt nếu nó có giá cả phải chăng. Apple cần duy trì truyền thống ra mắt sản phẩm ngay sau khi công bố, đặc biệt với một sản phẩm mới như iPhone Ultra. Tuy nhiên, nhiều người có thể sẵn lòng chờ đợi thêm một thời gian, nhất là khi Apple đã chậm chân trong lĩnh vực smartphone gập gần một thế kỷ.

article.title: Cơn ác mộng giá RAM sẽ không biến mất trước khi GTA VI lên PC
article.summary: Rockstar Games vừa phát hành video GTA VI: An Extended Look, mang đến cái nhìn rõ hơn về thế giới, nhân vật và lối chơi của bom tấn được chờ đợi suốt nhiều năm. Game dự kiến ra mắt trên PS5 và Xbox Series X|S vào ngày 19/11/2026, còn phiên bản PC vẫn chưa được công bố lịch phát hành.

sections.body: Rockstar Games vừa phát hành video GTA VI: An Extended Look, mang đến cái nhìn rõ hơn về thế giới, nhân vật và lối chơi của bom tấn được chờ đợi suốt nhiều năm. sections.heading: Các nguồn đang khớp nhau ở đâu
sections.body: Nếu Rockstar tiếp tục cách phát hành quen thuộc, game thủ PC có thể phải chờ thêm ít nhất một năm. GTA V lên máy tính khoảng 19 tháng sau bản console, trong khi Red Dead Redemption 2 cũng mất hơn một năm để thực hiện hành trình tương tự.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Thế nhưng đến lúc GTA VI đặt chân lên PC, người chơi có thể vẫn chưa thoát khỏi một vấn đề khác là giá bộ nhớ. CEO SK Hynix vừa cảnh báo tình trạng thiếu hụt chip nhớ có khả năng kéo dài đến hết năm 2030, còn năm 2027 có thể trở thành giai đoạn căng thẳng nhất. Nói theo cách quen thuộc của cộng đồng mạng, có lẽ chúng ta sẽ được chơi GTA VI trên PC trước khi RAM thực sự trở lại mức giá "ngon".

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Nhận định được ông Kwak Noh-Jung, CEO SK Hynix, đưa ra tại lễ khởi công cơ sở sản xuất bộ nhớ AI của hãng ở bang Indiana, Mỹ. Ông cho biết chưa nhìn thấy dấu hiệu rõ ràng cho thấy thị trường bộ nhớ sắp bước vào một chu kỳ giảm.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Theo Reuters, SK Hynix dự báo tình trạng thiếu hụt chip nhớ hiện nay sẽ kéo dài đến hết năm 2030. Sau thời điểm đó, nhu cầu có thể tăng chậm hơn nhưng khó giảm mạnh như những chu kỳ trước.

Theo Reuters, SK Hynix dự báo tình trạng thiếu hụt chip nhớ hiện nay sẽ kéo dài đến hết năm 2030. Sau thời điểm đó, nhu cầu có thể tăng chậm hơn nhưng khó giảm mạnh như những chu kỳ trước.

Tim Cook sẽ tiếp tục làm việc tại Apple với vai trò Chủ tịch điều hành và hỗ trợ công ty trong một số lĩnh vực, trong đó có làm việc với các nhà hoạch định chính sách trên toàn thế giới, theo thông báo của hãng “Táo khuyết”. Trong thời gian giữ chức CEO, Tim Cook đã giám sát quá trình Apple ra mắt nhiều sản phẩm mới, trong đó có Apple Watch, AirPods và gần đây là MacBook Neo. Ông cũng đóng vai trò quan trọng trong việc đưa doanh thu mảng Dịch vụ của Apple vượt mốc 100 tỷ USD, trở thành mảng kinh doanh lớn thứ hai của công ty, chỉ sau iPhone. CEO Tim Cook khi đến thăm Việt Nam năm 2024. Năm 2011, Tim Cook kế nhiệm Steve Jobs và trở thành CEO Apple. Trong thời gian lãnh đạo, vị CEO này tận dụng kinh nghiệm về chuỗi cung ứng để mở rộng đáng kể hoạt động kinh doanh của Apple. Vốn hóa thị trường của công ty tăng từ khoảng 350 tỷ USD lên hơn 4.000 tỷ USD, tương đương mức tăng khoảng 1.000%. Doanh thu hàng năm của Apple tăng mạnh, từ 108 tỷ USD năm 2011 lên 416 tỷ USD năm 2025. Riêng doanh thu iPhone tăng mạnh từ 47,1 tỷ USD lên 209,6 tỷ USD trong cùng giai đoạn. CEO Apple Tim Cook. (Ảnh: Getty) Apple Watch và AirPods cũng trở thành những sản phẩm đồng hồ thông minh và tai nghe phổ biến nhất thế giới. Một dấu ấn quan trọng khác của Tim Cook là thúc đẩy Apple chuyển từ chip Intel sang chip do hãng tự thiết kế cho dòng máy Mac. Việc tự phát triển chip giúp cải thiện đáng kể hiệu năng máy tính, đồng thời mang lại thời lượng pin vượt trội, lợi thế mà các đối thủ chỉ mới bắt kịp trong những năm gần đây. John Ternus tiếp quản vị trí CEO Apple trong bối cảnh công ty đang bước vào giai đoạn chuyển đổi lớn. Apple đang nỗ lực cải thiện năng lực trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) sau khi được cho là chậm chân hơn các đối thủ như Microsoft và Google. John Ternus và Tim Cook tại Apple Park. (Ảnh: Apple) Apple được kỳ vọng ra mắt phiên bản Siri mới sử dụng các mô hình AI Gemini của Google tại Hội nghị các nhà phát triển toàn cầu (WWDC) vào tháng 6. Bên cạnh đó, Apple được cho là đang chuẩn bị một trong những thay đổi lớn nhất đối với iPhone, với mẫu iPhone màn hình gập dự kiến ra mắt không lâu sau khi Tim Cook rời ghế CEO. Dưới thời Ternus, Apple cũng có thể trình làng kính thông minh và các sản phẩm tập trung vào AI nhằm cạnh tranh với những thiết bị AI thế hệ mới, trong đó có sản phẩm được OpenAI định hướng phát triển theo mô hình “AI-first”. Chặng đường mới của Apple dưới sự lãnh đạo của John Ternus sẽ chính thức bắt đầu từ ngày 1/9. Apple chuẩn bị sự kiện iPhone khác lạ nhất trong nhiều năm VOV.VN - Apple đã chốt ngày ra mắt iPhone mới, nhưng kế hoạch được cho là sẽ phá vỡ truyền thống giới thiệu toàn bộ dòng máy.

article.title: Con người nằm ở đâu trong vòng lặp bảo mật “có" AI?
article.summary: Sáng 05/08/2026, sự kiện BSides Hanoi lần thứ 2 chính thức diễn ra tại Hà Nội để tìm ra câu trả lời về mối quan hệ giữa con người và AI trong hệ thống bảo mật thời số hoá. Ông Vũ Duy Hiền, Phó Tổng thư ký kiêm Chánh Văn phòng Hiệp hội An ninh mạng Quốc gia phát biểu tại sự kiện.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: BSides Hanoi 2026 lần thứ 2 tổ chức tại Hà Nội với chủ đề "No Human", diễn ra trong tuần lễ chào mừng Ngày An ninh mạng Việt Nam 06/08. Chương trình năm nay trải rộng trên nhiều chủ đề, từ bảo mật blockchain, điều tra số trong kỷ nguyên Apple Intelligence, hoạt động của các nhóm tấn công có chủ đích (APT), phân tích mã độc, threat intelligence đến ứng dụng AI trong nghiên cứu và phòng thủ. Mỗi nghiên cứu tiếp cận một lát cắt khác nhau, nhưng khi đặt cạnh nhau lại phản ánh những chuyển dịch đang định hình an ninh mạng hiện đại.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Điểm chung đầu tiên là AI đang làm thay đổi cán cân giữa bên tấn công và bên phòng thủ. Những công nghệ giúp chuyên gia tăng tốc phân tích, tự động hóa quy trình và phát hiện mối đe dọa cũng đang được các nhóm tấn công khai thác để gia tăng tốc độ, quy mô và mức độ tinh vi của các chiến dịch. Cuộc cạnh tranh vì thế không còn nằm ở việc ai sở hữu AI, mà ở khả năng khai thác, kiểm soát và sử dụng AI hiệu quả hơn.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Được tổ chức bởi Công ty CP An ninh mạng Việt Nam (VSEC - thành viên của Tập đoàn Công nghệ G-Group), phối hợp cùng Hiệp hội An ninh mạng quốc gia (NCA) và Hiệp hội Internet Việt Nam (VIA), sự kiện tiếp tục mang tinh thần của chuỗi BSides toàn cầu – một diễn đàn cộng đồng, nơi các nhà nghiên cứu và chuyên gia chia sẻ nghiên cứu thực tiễn, phản biện các xu hướng mới và cùng tìm lời giải cho những thách thức của ngành.

Theo ông Trương Đức Lượng, Chủ tịch HĐQT VSEC và thành viên Hội đồng Chuyên môn, BSides được xây dựng như một nền tảng để kết nối cộng đồng bảo mật Việt Nam với cộng đồng quốc tế, khuyến khích chia sẻ tri thức và thúc đẩy sự phát triển bền vững của hệ sinh thái an ninh mạng.

article.summary: If Apple's iPhone Ultra has your attention, it's time to see what's been happening in the world of Android foldables for the past 8 years. sections.heading: Context: what is changing

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: This is going to drive a huge boost in sales for foldable phones , a category that has consistently grown since the first models arrived in 2019, but hasn't seen a particularly massive tentpole release like this one yet. Of course, as with anything Apple makes, you'll only get what Apple gives you, and rumor has it that Apple is announcing only one size and shape this time around.

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: But Android foldables, which have been around for eight years now, have had time to develop and branch out. Android offers a substantial choice of manufacturers, shapes, sizes, and capabilities that Apple simply can't offer. If foldable phones are looking like your next big purchase, here are many reasons you should choose an Android-powered one.

sections.heading: Who should pay attention now
sections.body: Folding phones usually come with two displays: an inner display and an outer display. The inner display is made of special ultrathin glass that can bend (unlike normal glass) and is reinforced with a preinstalled screen protector. The phone's frame is split into two halves connected by a specialized hinge, allowing you to open and close the phone.

sections.heading: What to watch next
sections.body: The foldable inner display is a special type of flexible OLED panel that's built to bend, too. A specialized hinge holds everything together, keeping dust and water out of the phone. It's a true marvel of engineering, and some foldables are even extremely durable, as proven by my Honor Magic V6 torture test .

draft_context.source_title: The rumored folding iPhone Ultra looks sick, but Android foldables offer something more: choice
draft_context.description: Rumor has it that Apple will announce the iPhone Ultra at its upcoming September 9 event, making it the first iPhone to sport an "ultra" moniker. We're not expecting it to push the boundaries of battery technology or camera prowess, but it is slated to do one big thing that no other iPhone has (intentionally) done: fold in half. This is going to drive a huge boost in sales for foldable phones , a category that has consistently grown since the first models arrived in 2019, but hasn't seen a particularly massive tentpole release like this one yet. Of course, as with anything Apple makes, you'll only get what Apple gives you, and rumor has it that Apple is announcing only one size and shape this time around. But Android foldables, which have been around for eight years now, have had time to develop and branch out. Android offers a substantial choice of manufacturers, shapes, sizes, and capabilities that Apple simply can't offer. If foldable phones are looking like your next big purchase, here are many reasons you should choose an Android-powered one. What is a folding phone and how do they work? (Image credit: Derrek Lee / Android Central) Folding phones usually come with two displays: an inner display and an outer display. The inner display is made of special ultrathin glass that can bend (unlike normal glass) and is reinforced with a preinstalled screen protector. The phone's frame is split into two halves connected by a specialized hinge, allowing you to open and close the phone. The foldable inner display is a special type of flexible OLED panel that's built to bend, too. A specialized hinge holds everything together, keeping dust and water out of the phone. It's a true marvel of engineering, and some foldables are even extremely durable, as proven by my Honor Magic V6 torture test . Both the inner and outer displays work the same way a regular smartphone touchscreen does. You can open apps on either of them, allowing you to choose the size of the "canvas" you want to view them on. What types of folding phones exist (and why would someone want one)? The rumored iPhone Ultra. (Image credit: AppleTrack) The leaked image of the iPhone Ultra above shows what's known as a book-style foldable. When a book-style phone is closed, its size and shape are similar to those of a standard smartphone, so all your favorite apps look and feel nearly identical to those on your existing smartphone. Opening a book-style phone doubles its size, turning it into a small tablet that lets you get more done without switching to a laptop or other computer. I work on the go quite a bit, and a folding phone makes it easy to get most of my work done efficiently. I rarely watch videos on my phone, but when I do, the extra-large inner display is a real treat. Because of the large size, multitasking is one of the best features of a book-style foldable. You can run two or three apps side by side on these phones, and even put apps in floating windows, like on a laptop OS. Plus, the taskbar on the inner display makes it feel even more like a multitasking beast, similar to a laptop OS (like Windows or macOS). Book-style foldables come in many sizes and shapes, though most are slightly taller and narrower than your average smartphone when closed. Google began its foldable journey with a shorter, wider model , but made the next three entries a bit taller. Meanwhile, Samsung just introduced its first shorter, wider model (the Galaxy Z Fold 8 ), and Apple's iPhone Ultra is rumored to use this same size and shape. Shorter, wider models are best for video content and feel a lot like holding a small TV when unfolded. Apple's iPhone Ultra is said to come in just one shape and size, while Android foldables offer tons of different sizes, shapes, and form factors. You can even get tri-fold foldables ! (Image credit: Android Central) While book-style foldables get the bulk of the attention, flip-style foldables were better sellers for a few years. Phones like the Motorola Razr 2026 series look like a slightly taller normal smartphone when opened, then fold into a perfectly pocketable half-sized phone when closed. These phones solve the issue of overly large phones while still giving you the flexibility to use a small screen for things like notifications and messaging, then a larger screen when you need it. We generally recommend Motorola's Razr flip phones over Samsung's Z Flip line because Motorola's outer screen is more capable , and the company's designs are far more interesting. Flip phones are also wonderful for photos and videos thanks to their shape. It's easy to bend a flip phone at a 90-degree angle and use it as a "tripod" to take group photos. You can also use this same shape and hold it sideways to take video like a classic camcorder. Do folding phones have any downsides? (Image credit: Nicholas Sutrich) Folding phones offer unique form factors and ways to interact with your favorite apps, but not everything is a win-win. When shopping for a book-style folding phone, the first thing you'll probably notice is the price. Yeah, there's quite a bit of sticker shock here, and that's mainly because this is a two-in-one device. Think of it as buying a phone and a tablet at the same time, and you'll understand. Flip-style phones are typically priced the same as traditional flagship phones but tend to have one fewer rear camera. Even Motorola's Razr Ultra line doesn't have a third camera on the back, despite the higher price. Both flip and book-style foldables are often a bit less powerful than top-tier traditional flagship smartphones. The problem is that there's not as much space in these phones for cooling, since they have to be thinner than a traditional phone to avoid feeling like a brick when closed. (Image credit: Nicholas Sutrich / Android Central) Lastly, durability. Folding phones got a bad rap pretty early on when the original Galaxy Z Fold's inner display would spontaneously break, but those problems have generally been solved. There's always a chance the folding glass could break, but these phones have undergone so many years of evolution and hardening that such a failure is almost unheard of. Stores like uBreakiFix readily have parts to repair them, and phone companies offer warranties and other insurance programs that help cover any potential issues. As someone who has reviewed dozens and dozens of folding phones over the past seven years, I've never seen a phone break in person. My wife has also been using flip phones for the past four years, and the only time one of hers broke was after being dropped with the phone unfolded. Considering how many traditional smartphones break every day from drops, there's no reason to suggest that these phones are any less durable with regular use. ]]>

draft_context.source_title: Get ready, Apple’s iPhone event is massive this year
draft_context.description: Macworld Apple always holds its events at 10 am PT, with iPhone launches usually taking place on the second Tuesday or Wednesday of September. This year, that means the event, dubbed Surprise and Shine , will take place on Wednesday, September 9. Additionally, Apple always introduces its new iPhones and Apple Watches at its September special event, and this year is no different. Except this year, everything is different. The iPhones are different . The CEO is different . The event may be different. Here’s what we expect from Apple’s big September show. The John Ternus show Tim Cook stepped down from his position as CEO after 15 years, though he will remain on the board of directors. He has named John Ternus, who was most recently senior vice president of hardware engineering, as his successor. That means this is the first Apple Special Event in which Ternus will be the headliner, introducing the start of the event and thanking everyone at the end. Individual products are likely to be demonstrated by other Apple executives—they always are—but this is a big opportunity to shake up the format of Apple events in general. Will we see a return to live stage events ? Will the structure and format of the pre-recorded video events change at all? Or will Ternus be essentially interchangeable for Tim Cook, with nothing else about these big product reveals changing at all? Will Apple make a “Turn” pun at some point? We’ll have to wait and see. iPhone Ultra For the first time in over a decade, Apple is going to dramatically change the iPhone’s form factor. Apple is going to release a folding iPhone, which most are expecting to be called iPhone Ultra. It will fold in half like a book and be shaped sort of like a passport when closed; an unusual aspect ratio for any phone and especially an iPhone. This should be the relative size and shape of the folding iPhone Ultra. Foundry We expect two cameras (wide and ultrawide) on the back, one on the front, and the reintroduction of Touch ID in the side button for authentication. This is going to be a very premium product, with most rumors citing a starting price of $2,000 or more. Not much is known about the software experience, though. Obviously, Apple will need to change some of how iOS looks and feels, and offer impressive new software features, to justify a folding phone with displays on the outside and inside and all new aspect ratios and sizes. Check out our roundup of rumors about the iPhone Ultra for more. iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max The iPhone Ultra won’t be the only high-priced iPhone hitting the market this fall. With the standard iPhone 18 supposedly getting bumped back to a spring release, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are going to be the only other iPhones launched this fall. We expect an upgraded A20 Pro processor , a better modem (the C2 in many countries, possibly a Qualcomm modem in the U.S.), and a new Dark Cherry signature color . A dark red/cherry color should be the signature shade of the iPhone 18 Pro, along with Light Blue, Dark Gray, and Silver. Foundry For the most part, the iPhone 18 Pro will resemble the iPhone 17 Pro, but there should be a big upgrade to the rear camera (variable aperture, new sensor technology) and possibly a boost to 24 megapixels for the front camera. Battery capacity may go up by 6-8 percent, which could lead to longer battery life in conjunction with other improvements and optimizations. Check out our roundup of rumors about the iPhone 18 Pro for more. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 Apple always updates its Apple Watch line at the same time as the iPhone, whether it needs to or not. That means that this year, we’ll see the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Ultra 4. So far, none of the rumors suggest much of a change from the previous model. There will be a somewhat faster S12 processor, but major new health features or other changes don’t seem to be in the cards this year. Rumors say there won’t be a new SE 4 this year. Apple TV and Homepod mini Both long overdue for an update, Apple has been waiting to release a new Apple TV 4K set-top box and the HomePod mini until it figured out how to really make the new Siri work. Now, with a whole new Siri architecture coming in the OS 27 updates this fall, it’s finally ready to ship these products. Because Apple TV set-top boxes and HomePods act as a “home hub” for Apple’s smart home controls, Apple needed to make sure they’re capable of running the all-new Siri. That said, we haven’t heard of any major new software features that make use of the improved hardware coming to Apple TV or HomePod. These new products will give you the new Siri experience just as a modern Apple Watch will, but the tvOS interface and features probably won’t get a big change. It’s more like: you’ll ask Siri something, and you’ll get Siri AI answers, not the old Siri. Foundry HomePad preview The new Apple TV and HomePod mini will mark the start of a bigger, more ambitious smart home plan for Apple that all revolves around the new Siri and the expanded AI features that will be built out on top of it in the coming months and years. The main device we’re waiting for is the so-called HomePad smart hub that has long been rumored. The device is expected to have an iPad-like squarish screen that can either hang on a wall or dock to a speaker. It will reportedly run a new operating system dubbed HomeOS that is powered by Siri AI. In his August 9 Power On newsletter , Mark Gurman reported that “a September preview of that product is plausible.” That could very well be Ternus’ surprise “One more Thing” to close the show. However, it is unlikely to go on sale until later in 2026 or early 2027.

draft_context.description: I've been following this story for a while, but it seems like Call of Duty fans of at least one of their PC versions have cause to celebrate this week. Microsoft has been hard at work leveraging its Call of Duty acquisition to boost Xbox's fortunes in recent years, shipping Black Ops 1 and 2 "classic" versions exclusively onto PlayStation to huge fanfare. Indeed, the "classic" Call of Duty versions have been in the spotlight somewhat lately, as fans clamor for an era of a more grounded, less microtransaction-laden Call of Duty. Modern versions are replete with pop culture bloat and mountains of "features" nobody really asked for, leaving nostalgic millennials and older gen-z players yearning for simpler times. Of course, you can always play the classic Call of Duty games on PC via Steam or on Xbox Series X|S via backwards compatibility. The downside is that these classic Call of Duty versions are often infested with aimbot hackers at best, and RCE vulnerabilities at worst . Remote Code Execution (RCE) exploits allow players in multiplayer titles to literally upload malware to your computer. The way some older games work with regard to peer-to-peer networking, if left unpatched, facilitate this malignant type of attack. Modern Warfare 2 on PC has been notorious for these types of vulnerabilities unfortunately, but there may be light at the end of the tunnel. In a statement to Windows Central, Activision claimed the following: " An update released this week addressed all known vulnerabilities in Modern Warfare 2. The team continues to support our legacy titles, with additional updates coming soon. We encourage anyone aware of additional issues to report them through Activision's Bug Bounty Portal ." There are other reports of aimbots, wall hacks, and even RCE exploits in other classic Call of Duty PC games, but it sounds as though Activision is now actively working through these after realizing the potential goldmine it's sitting on. Indeed, Call of Duty: Black Ops 1 and 2 dominated the PlayStation store over the summer, potentially opening up new revenue streams for the legendary franchise. What about Call of Duty on Xbox backwards compatibility? Classic Call of Duty games are available on Xbox backwards compatibility ... but it's a double edged sword somewhat. (Image credit: Activision) I've also requested for Activision to comment on the Xbox backwards compatible versions of Call of Duty, which are similarly replete with hackers and aimbots and the like. Xbox backwards compatibility is one of the best features Xbox Series X|S and Xbox One have in my view. It allows hundreds of classic Xbox and Xbox 360 games to carry forward, ensuring that your purchases travel with you. In the early days, having all of the classic Call of Duty titles in one place is arguably a huge selling point for Xbox as a console ecosystem. However, Microsoft itself offered a huge flaw in the system this summer, when it ported the classic Black Ops 1 and 2 exclusively to PlayStation, complete with modernized security updates and server infrastructure. It's a sad state of affairs for Xbox fans of classic Call of Duty games potentially. Despite Xbox literally owning Call of Duty, Xbox fans are left with the worst experience thanks to the unpatched security vulnerabilities. Since the classic Call of Duty titles available on Xbox Series X|S today are effectively Xbox 360 versions, the source code of which is likely archived, it seems incredibly unlikely Microsoft and Activision will be willing to patch some of these. The Xbox 360 security layers are easily bypassed these days, with modded consoles opening up old school backwards compatible multiplayer titles to a variety of vulnerabilities. It's a sad state of affairs for Xbox fans of classic Call of Duty games potentially. Despite Xbox literally owning Call of Duty, Xbox fans are left with the worst experience thanks to the unpatched security vulnerabilities. I'll update this article if Activision responds to my queries on the topic, but at least for now, PC players of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 should feel a bit safer for the time being. article.title: Is Apple working on its own game controller?
article.summary: According to a sharp-eyed MacRumors reader , the first macOS 26.7 release candidate included references to a pair of game controllers. The same release candidate included code numbers for a slew of other in-development Apple products .
article.dek: According to a sharp-eyed MacRumors reader , the first macOS 26.7 release candidate included references to a pair of game controllers.
article.hook: According to a sharp-eyed MacRumors reader , the first macOS 26.7 release candidate included references to a pair of game controllers.

sections.heading: Context: what is changing
sections.body: According to a sharp-eyed MacRumors reader , the first macOS 26.7 release candidate included references to a pair of game controllers. The same release candidate included code numbers for a slew of other in-development Apple products .

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: The two hardware devices are referenced as T6502 and T1057 and they include most standard game controller features: dual thumbsticks, face buttons, triggers, home and menu buttons, and different haptic features. One notable difference: the T1057 controller includes gryscope and accelerometer support (so games can tell how you tilt or move the controller) while T6502 does not.

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: While this is an interesting find, I caution readers not to assume that Apple is working on its own game controller. There have been rumors of Apple making its own game controller for over a decade, and nothing has ever come of it. Apple has instead done a lot to provide proper support for third-party game controllers, whether that’s its own MFi program or controllers for home console systems.

sections.heading: Who should pay attention now
sections.body: For years, you have been able to sync an Xbox or PlayStation controller to your Apple devices, including iPhones, iPads, Macs, and Apple TV. That includes the latest controllers for the Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5.

sections.heading: What to watch next
sections.body: These code numbers probably reference test devices that are used in testing support for core game controller functions, or legacy references to R&D projects for Apple game controllers that may never be built. Apple famously has many products in various stages of development and only a few of them are ever released.

There have been rumors of Apple making its own game controller for over a decade, and nothing has ever come of it. Apple has instead done a lot to provide proper support for third-party game controllers, whether that’s its own MFi program or controllers for home console systems. For years, you have been able to sync an Xbox or PlayStation controller to your Apple devices, including iPhones, iPads, Macs, and Apple TV. That includes the latest controllers for the Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5. These code numbers probably reference test devices that are used in testing support for core game controller functions, or legacy references to R&D projects for Apple game controllers that may never be built. Apple famously has many products in various stages of development and only a few of them are ever released. Apple could be building its own game controller, but there would be little reason to. Find My support and automatic switching between devices would be useful, but it’s hard to argue that modern controllers are missing features that require Apple to do its own thing. It makes much more sense for Apple to support the tens of millions of Xbox and PlayStation controllers than to make its own, especially as Apple’s platforms are not very popular for the kinds of games one usually plays with controllers.
